summary: The note describes how space weather-driven ionospheric disturbances degrade high-frequency (HF) radio communications, citing events in 2023 such as a geomagnetic storm and a disruption of transatlantic flight radio links. It covers progress in forecasting, resilient transceiver technology, international regulation, and workforce and public education. The overall outlook is cautiously optimistic, though the unpredictability of space weather remains a challenge.
one_line: Ionospheric disturbances from space weather threaten HF radio communications, prompting advances in forecasting, resilient equipment, regulation, and training.
key_facts: On October 5, 2023, a spike in solar activity triggered a moderate geomagnetic storm, with auroras sighted as far south as Colorado.
The ionosphere is the layer of Earth's atmosphere charged by solar radiation and essential for HF radio wave propagation.

On September 15, 2023, a significant ionospheric disturbance disrupted HF radio links used for transatlantic flights, and pilots lost contact with air traffic control intermittently and switched to backup protocols.
John Richardson, a pilot with Atlantic Airlines, said the radios 'crackled and died' midway over the ocean and that satellite phones, which they relied on, also have limitations.

Dr. Emily Carter of the Global Space Weather Monitoring Network says solar flares can shift the ionosphere's density and composition unpredictably, rapidly reducing the reliability of radio communication and navigation systems.

On December 6, 2023, a team led by Dr. Miguel Alvarez of the Ionospheric Forecasting Initiative announced a successful test of a machine-learning algorithm using real-time solar data that gives a 72-hour forecast with improved accuracy.
On February 12, 2024, Radiocom Solutions unveiled its 'ResilientHF' transceivers, built to operate under adverse ionospheric conditions.
Maria Green, CTO of Radiocom Solutions, says the devices integrate adaptive frequency selection and enhanced error correction for real-time adjustments.
At the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference on April 3, 2024, a global framework for sharing space weather information and best practices for protecting HF communication infrastructure was ratified.
Regulators in several countries are moving to mandate that aviation and maritime industries adopt technologies mitigating ionospheric disturbances, expected to take effect by mid-2025.
Pilot training programs now include space weather modules, and maritime academies have revised curricula to cover ionospheric disturbances.
The Space Weather Outreach Foundation leads public campaigns of lectures, workshops, and interactive experiences about space weather.
